entry.title: Somalia expels the UAE’s ambassador, accusing Abu Dhabi of an "open invasion"
entry.content:
Mogadishu on Thursday gave the Emirati diplomat 72 hours to leave the country and recalled its own envoy. The federal government accuses Abu Dhabi of backing the regions that defy it.

Somalia’s information minister, Abdifatah Kasim Mohamud, announced through the state news agency on Thursday November 19th that the ambassador of the United Arab Emirates had 72 hours to leave the country and that Mogadishu was recalling its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, denouncing an "open invasion". Two days earlier the president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, had accused the Emirates of giving economic and political backing to regional administrations opposed to the federal government and of signing deals with them over the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo. Abu Dhabi, which denies any interference, calls the move "hostile" and regrets being dragged into Somalia’s power struggles, even as the Emirates still fund some 3,400 Somali troops around the capital, according to sources quoted by Reuters.

entry.title: Somalia’s Supreme Court rules the extension of the president’s term unlawful
entry.content:
The country’s highest court on Thursday gave the parties thirty days to reach agreement and ninety days to hold elections. The day before, the head of state, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, had sacked the chief justice.

On Thursday 5 November the constitutional chamber of Somalia’s Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional amendments adopted in March could extend neither the term of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, which expired on 15 May, nor that of parliament, and confined the federal government to a caretaker role. The day before, the president had sacked the chief justice, Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, who was hearing an opposition challenge, and replaced him with a close ally, Ibrahim Idle Suleiman; the court declared the dismissal void, and the former prime minister Hassan Ali Khaire accuses the government of sending soldiers into the courthouse. The judges demand an agreement between political parties within thirty days and elections within ninety, whereas the president meant to lead the country to its first direct elections, planned for April and May 2027, a reform whose terms the opposition and several regional parties dispute.
